33:2.text: Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.

provenance.other: “search the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The phrase had become detached devotional English well before 1830, which is why Alma 14:1's use of it is held at moderate; this row is stronger because of what follows it, not because of the words.
provenance.significance: John 5:39 gives a reason for searching the scriptures — 'they are they which testify of me' — and Alma 33 is that reason executed at length. From 33:3 to 33:19 the chapter does nothing but produce witnesses: Zenos, then Zenock, then Moses, each introduced as having spoken of the Son of God, with 33:14 asking outright 'if ye have read the Scriptures? If ye have, how can ye disbelieve on the Son of God?' That is John 5:39's clause turned into a syllogism. Compare Hays on metalepsis: what the borrowed imperative suppresses is the ground of the imperative, and Alma spends seventeen verses supplying it.

33:2.note: 'Ye do greatly err, and ye had ought to search the Scriptures.' Three words of a KJV singleton, in its imperative sense rather than Alma 14:1's narrative one ('began … to search the Scriptures'). The row is written in full rather than cross-referenced back to 14:1 because the second use is the argument: John 5:39 says the scriptures testify of Christ, and Alma 33:3-19 is a catalogue of scriptures testifying of Christ, ending at 33:14 with the inference John's clause licenses.

33:2.text: He is not the God of the dead, but the God of the living: ye therefore do greatly err.

provenance.other: “do greatly err” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 12:27, which closes the exchange that Mark 12:24 opens: 'Do ye not therefore err, because ye know not the scriptures, neither the power of God?'
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons stand in this one sentence and they come from two different arguments about scripture. What Mark supplies is the diagnosis Alma needs and the shape of it: erring, and erring specifically from not knowing the scriptures. Recover the context and the Sadducees are being answered on the resurrection — they had constructed an absurdity out of the law to prove the resurrection false, and Jesus tells them the fault is in their reading. Alma's hearers have constructed an absurdity out of a building to prove they cannot worship, and get the same answer. The parallel extends to the remedy: Mark 12:26 begins 'have ye not read in the book of Moses', and Alma 33:19 ends with Moses.

33:2.note: 'If ye suppose that ye cannot worship God, ye do greatly err, and ye had ought to search the Scriptures; for if ye suppose that they have taught you this, ye do not understand them.' The three-word run is a KJV singleton, and the clause it belongs to in Mark is 'ye know not the scriptures' — which is the second half of Alma's sentence, given as 'ye do not understand them'. Mark 12:24 and 12:27 are the bookends of a single reply and the Book of Mormon has both ends of it in one verse, in Mark's own order: err, then scriptures, then a charge of not understanding.

33:7.text: But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret; and thy Father which seeth in secret shall reward thee openly.

provenance.other: “into thy closet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “seen of men” occurs in exactly two, Matthew 6:5 and Matthew 23:5, both of them indictments of display. The KJV's 'closet' elsewhere is Joel 2:16's bridal chamber, which has nothing to do with prayer.
provenance.significance: This is the answer to Alma 31, and it is Matthew's. The Zoramites pray standing on a platform in a synagogue, once a week, in a voice loud enough for a crowd; Matthew 6:5 describes hypocrites who 'love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men'; and Matthew 6:6 gives the alternative, which is the closet with the door shut. The prophecy Alma produces to prove that the expelled poor can still worship is a prayer whose sequence runs wilderness, field, house, closet — four places, none of them a synagogue, and the last of them the KJV's one word for private prayer. Two chapters of narrative set up a problem that a pair of consecutive Sermon on the Mount verses solves, with the Sermon's own vocabulary and without naming it.

33:7.note: 'And when I did turn unto my closet, O Lord, and prayed unto thee, thou didst hear me.' Three words of a KJV singleton attached to the KJV's own verb of praying, inside a text the chapter attributes to a prophet of old. The next verse completes the pair: 'when they cry unto thee to be heard of thee, and not of men' inverts Matthew 6:5's 'that they may be seen of men' — Alma keeps the construction and changes the sense from sight to hearing, which is the change the whole Zenos prayer is built on, since every stanza of it turns on 'thou didst hear me'. The Zenos text has no biblical original and is not extant outside the Book of Mormon; what can be said is that its distinctive vocabulary at this point is Matthew's.

33:11.text: The LORD hath taken away thy judgments, he hath cast out thine enemy: the king of Israel, even the LORD, is in the midst of thee: thou shalt not see evil any more.

provenance.other: “taken away thy judgments” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the only place in the KJV where God's judgments are removed from a person rather than executed. The Book of Mormon reads 'turned thy judgments away from me', which keeps the noun and the removal and changes the verb.
provenance.significance: Zephaniah 3:15 puts two things in one sentence — the judgments taken away, and the enemy cast out — and Alma 33:10-11 has both in the same order, with the casting out reassigned: 'thou hast also heard me when I have been cast out, and have been despised by mine enemies … thou hast turned thy judgments away from me.' In the prophet it is the enemy who is cast out; in Zenos it is the speaker, by his enemies. That reassignment is the whole point of quoting Zenos to this congregation, since the men Alma is preaching to have just been cast out of their synagogue (33:2), and the verse tells them that the one whose judgments were turned away was the one who was thrown out. Alma repeats the clause at 33:13 as the single thing his hearers must believe, and attaches to it the reason Zephaniah does not give: 'because of thy Son'.

33:11.note: 'Thou hast turned thy judgments away from me, because of thy Son.' The KJV removes judgments from a person exactly once, at Zephaniah 3:15, and that verse also supplies the casting out of an enemy which stands one verse earlier in Alma. No run survives — 'turned … away' for 'taken away' is a real departure, and 'turned away' by itself is formulaic across twenty-four KJV verses — so the row rests on the collocation rather than on the wording. Recorded at moderate.
33:11.whyNot: Judgments turned away is ordinary prophetic English (compare Isaiah 12:1's 'thine anger is turned away'), and the Zenos prayer is a composed text whose phrases may be assembled from the Book of Mormon's own idiom rather than from any one verse.

33:19.text: And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live.

provenance.route: Numbers 21:8-9 read through John 3:14-15 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Numbers 21:8 supplies the looking and the living — 'when he looketh upon it, shall live' — and John 3:14-15 supplies the frame: 'as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness … That whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have eternal life.' mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence, because the two texts do not compete at any point: the Book of Mormon has parts of both. The call is therefore made by eye, on two words. 'In the wilderness' stands in John and not in Numbers, whose setting is the wilderness but whose sentence does not say so; and 'whosoever' is John's, where Numbers has 'every one that is bitten'. Alma's own verb, 'raised up', is in neither — it is Deuteronomy 18's word for the prophet, and it is the seam between this row and the next. “looketh upon it” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Numbers 21:8 and Isaiah 28:4, and only the first has anyone live by it; “serpent in the wilderness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 3:14.
provenance.alternative: Numbers 21:8-9 alone accounts for the looking and the living, and the Book of Mormon could reach the christological reading through its own earlier use of the type rather than through John.
provenance.significance: Alma does not mention a serpent. He says 'a type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live' — which presupposes that his hearers know what was raised up, and simultaneously presupposes John's reading of it, since Numbers offers no ground for calling the pole a type of anything. What the verse borrows from John is not wording but permission: John 3:14 is the text that makes Numbers 21 available as a prophecy of the Son of God, and Alma 33:19 uses it as such while quoting the Old Testament. The chapter then does something John does not: 33:20-21 asks why anyone would refuse to look, and answers that they did not believe it would heal them — which converts the type from a promise into a diagnosis of unbelief, and hands Alma the transition back to his seed.

33:19.note: 'A type was raised up in the wilderness, that whosoever would look upon it might live. And many did look and live.' The looking and the living are Numbers 21:8's, in Numbers' order; the wilderness and the 'whosoever' are John 3:14-15's. Hardy's apparatus cross-references Numbers 21:4-9 at 33:20, the verse in which the refusal to look is explained; the wording is at 33:19 and the link is filed there, with 33:20-21 carried in the recurrence list — see the exclusion register at 33:20. Mediation is recorded as OT-via-NT on a judgment rather than on a machine result, and the two words carrying it are named above so the call can be disputed.

33:19.text: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken;

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 18:15-18, or its quotation at Acts 3:22-23 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: mediation-check.py was run twice on this verse and returned no decisive divergence either time — Deuteronomy 18:15 against Acts 3:22, and Deuteronomy 18:19 against Acts 3:23 — because Alma 33:19-20 reproduces nothing at any point where the two differ. The one word held in common with both is 'raise up' / 'raised up', and it is common to both, so it discriminates nothing. Contrast 1 Nephi 22:20, where twenty-six continuous words settle the same question decisively for Acts.
provenance.significance: The claim 'he was spoken of by Moses' is not a quotation; it is a title deed, and Deuteronomy 18:15-18 is the deed. It is the one place in the Pentateuch where Moses is made to speak of a coming figure, and Acts 3:22 is the New Testament's own citation of it, introduced with a formula Alma's clause resembles in substance — 'For Moses truly said unto the fathers.' What is worth recording is the difference between this verse and 1 Nephi 22:20. Nephi quotes the prophecy; Alma asserts it and moves immediately to the brazen serpent, a passage in which Moses does not speak of anyone. Alma 33:19 uses Deuteronomy 18 as a warrant rather than as a text, and that is a different relation to scripture from the one the same book displays at its opening.

33:19.note: Filed to discharge a Hardy cross-reference (PLAN §7.2) that has been checked against the printed page and confirmed correctly keyed: the footnote sits on 'he was spoken of by Moses' in this verse, and the row is not a parser artifact. Our own reading is that there is no verbal borrowing here, so the link is figural and the confidence is moderate — the reference is right about what Alma is claiming and cannot be shown from the wording. Not to be read as a second instance of the 1 Nephi 22:20 quotation; the recurrence list points there so that a reader can see what the same source looks like when the Book of Mormon does quote it.
33:19.whyNot: There is no shared wording at all beyond 'raise up', which stands in both candidates and in hundreds of other KJV verses. Alma 33:19 names Moses and then quotes Numbers, not Deuteronomy. If the Hardy row were withdrawn, nothing in the verse would generate this link on its own evidence, and it should be withdrawn if the brazen serpent is judged to exhaust the reference to Moses.

33:23.text: For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.

provenance.other: “burden is light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “lowly in heart” — used at Alma 32:8 — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the verse immediately before it.
provenance.significance: The sermon is bracketed by two consecutive verses of Matthew 11. Alma opened at 32:8 by telling the expelled poor 'I behold that ye are lowly in heart', which is Matthew 11:29's description of Christ himself; he closes here by praying 'that your burdens may be light', which is Matthew 11:30's promise about what following that Christ costs. Between them stands the whole seed allegory. Recover the source's context and the invitation the two verses complete is 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' — addressed, in Alma, to people who have just told him they have nowhere to worship and no one to hear them. The bracket is not stated by either text and is not likely to be accidental: the two KJV singletons involved sit next to each other in Matthew and at the two ends of one sermon in Alma.

33:23.note: 'And then may God grant unto you that your burdens may be light, through the joy of his Son.' Three words of a KJV singleton, in the same figurative sense, closing the discourse whose opening greeting came from the preceding verse of the same Matthean saying. Alma adds the agent Matthew leaves implicit — the burden is light 'through the joy of his Son' — which is the chapter's governing addition to everything it borrows, since 33:11 and 33:13 make 'because of thy Son' the clause Zenos's prayer turns on as well.
